title: Technical deep dive - Autoscaling & capacity planning
transcript: [00:00:00] Meeting header: 2025-04-10 15:00 UTC Duration 54m; Attendees: Ivy, Markus (Redwood); Lena, Samir, Priya, Ben (Arbor)
[00:00:08] Ivy: hey everyone thanks for joining, gonna do a deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning we've got Markus to dig into numbers.
[00:00:15] Lena: yeah thanks, we've been running the hosted API in prod for a few weeks and want to understand burst behavior and reserved gpu planning for critical flows

[00:00:28] Samir: high level constraint: 99th p99 latency target 150ms for short chat paths, but we have big peaks (batch of 600 concurrent small calls) during morning syncs, so wondering best burst policy
[00:00:45] Markus: cool  we'll go through queueing models, burst policies, reserved vs on-demand GPUs, and how KV cache + batching affects throughput and tail latency
[00:01:10] Ivy: quick note  we've shared a capacity spreadsheet and an autoscale playbook link in the chat (see  -> /docs/capacity-playbook), will reference that
[00:01:35] Ben: quick context: most calls are 128 token average, some long form 1k token reports but those are <5% of traffic
[00:01:48] Markus: great, that's the right mix  smaller seq len favors throughput optimizations and batching, long tails affect memory (kv cache) and can block GPUs if not handled
[00:02:10] Priya: security question up front: for Private deployments we need KMS integration and audit logs; does autoscaling trigger any extra artifacts?
[00:02:25] Ivy: autoscaling operations are logged and we can push to your SIEM; scaling events and model rollouts are also in audit trail  for Private on-prem we can route logs to your Kinesis/Splunk
[00:02:40] Lena: ok good. let's move to queueing  do you have a simple queuing model that maps incoming RPS to GPU counts?

[00:02:55] Markus: yes  we typically model requests with an M/M/c-ish approximation but add a service time distribution informed by token counts, quantization, and batching. Short version: required gpus = ceil((arrival_rate * avg_service_time) / concurrency_per_gpu).
[00:03:20] Samir: concurrency_per_gpu meaning how many simultaneous decodes a single GPU can handle given batching?

[00:03:28] Markus: exactly  depends on sequence lengths, model size, whether kv cache hits happen, and quantization level. For a 70B quantized to 4-bit we see higher concurrency than fp16 on same hw. We've got empirical profiles in that spreadsheet
[00:04:05] Ben: you said kv cache hits  how does cache hit rate change needed capacity?

[00:04:12] Markus: good q  high prefix reuse (KV hits) reduces compute per request because we avoid re-encoding earlier tokens; effectively lowers avg service time for subsequent tokens. So if you have conversational flows that hit cache 60-80% after warmup, your effective capacity goes up significantly
[00:04:45] Lena: what's the recommended warmup window and how do you handle cold starts for canary traffic?

[00:04:52] Markus: autoscaler can keep a small pool of warm workers (min replicas) for low-latency SLOs; for canaries we recommend pinned instances or burst pool so cold-starts don't affect p99. Warmup depends on model  for large models 30-60s to populate kv for typical session, smaller models faster
[00:05:20] Samir: explain burst pools  are those reserved GPUs or ephemeral?

[00:05:27] Markus: both options. Bursts can be served by reserved capacity you own (Dedicated GPUs) or by a burst pool that spins up on-demand (hosted). Tradeoff: reserved guarantees latency and avoids warmup but costs more; hosted burst is cheaper but may have ~1-2 minute spin-up depending on infra and image caching
[00:06:00] Ivy: also we support hybrid: keep small reserved baseline for SLO-critical flows and use hosted burst for overflow. Routing policies can send critical routes to reserved first.
[00:06:18] Priya: for Private/VPC deployments, can we still use hosted burst? security concerns on mixing?

[00:06:25] Markus: Private can use on-prem burst only; however you can configure a secure peering to a cloud burst cluster if permitted by your compliance team. Otherwise, Dedicated Reserved + autoscale within VPC is typical
[00:06:50] Lena: let's talk numbers  assume morning peak 600 concurrent short calls with 128 tokens avg. What baseline reserved GPUs would you recommend?

[00:07:00] Markus: with our profiling for a 70B quantized model on A100-class GPU, typical concurrency per GPU for 128 tokens is ~40-60 requests (depends on batching latency budget). Using conservative 40, 600/40 = 15 GPUs. With headroom for spikes and 99pct SLO we recommend 18 reserved and rely on burst to reach 25 if needed. We'll send you the precise calc in the sheet
[00:07:35] Samir: that seems high we're thinking maybe 8 reserved and let autoscale handle the rest, but concerned about p99 spikes

[00:07:43] Markus: that's the tradeoff; if you keep 8 reserved, your overflow will route to burst with potential warm starts and queueing. Queueing models show p99 can jump if queue length grows; we can set max_queue_ms and give callers a fast-fail or degrade to smaller model to maintain latency
[00:08:10] Ben: can Redwood automatically fallback to a smaller model when queuing?
[00:08:16] Ivy: yes  routing policies support model variant fallbacks and graceful degradation; we can configure automatic reroute to 13B quantized variant for non-critical requests
[00:08:30] Lena: how do batching knobs affect this? I'm worried increasing batch windows hurts p50 but helps throughput

[00:08:38] Markus: exactly  batching window trades latency for throughput. For interactive SLO you keep batching windows minimal (5-15ms) and rely on concurrency; for non-interactive or background tasks you can allow higher batching windows (50-200ms) to reduce GPU count. Our optimizer suggests dynamic batch windows per route
[00:09:05] Priya: are there any security implications of caching KV across sessions? tenant isolation?

[00:09:12] Markus: KV cache is per-session/tenant; we never mix across customers. For private deployments you control persistent cache policies. Cache eviction and retention can be tuned some customers prefer no persistent caching for regulated data
[00:09:40] Samir: what about quantization tradeoffs  if we quantize more aggressively we can reduce GPUs but lose some quality on safety prompts

[00:09:48] Markus: yes that's the QA tradeoff. 4-bit qlora variants often preserve most quality; we ship evals and regression tests. For safety-critical flows, keep fp16 or higher precision; for lower-risk features, 4-bit gives large capacity wins
[00:10:15] Lena: can you show a sample scaling policy config?

[00:10:20] Markus: sure  (walkthrough) debounce scaling to avoid oscillation, set min_replicas to reserved baseline, scale_up_threshold at 70% GPU utilization and scale_down after sustained below 40% for 2 minutes. We also support rate-based scaling: e.g., scale to maintain queue length < 50ms
[00:11:05] Ivy: note we recommend combining utilization and queue-length signals, because utilization alone misses bursty arrivals that spike queueing
[00:11:22] Ben: how are cold caches handled during scale-up? will new workers be warmed before traffic lands?

[00:11:30] Markus: two strategies: pre-warm with synthetic traffic or keep a small warm standby. Pre-warm is useful for known scheduled peaks; standby is better for unpredictable spikes but costs reserved capacity
[00:11:52] Samir: our infra team is concerned about cost predictability  we prefer reserved predictable spend. Any hybrid recommendations?

[00:11:58] Markus: hybrid baseline + burst is the standard: baseline sized to meet 95-99% of expected steady demand; burst handles tail. We can estimate cost delta and show ROI for reducing reserved vs upping burst budget
[00:12:20] Lena: want to dig into queueing math quickly  what's the expected p99 increase if queue grows from 50ms to 500ms?

[00:12:28] Markus: p99 is sensitive  example: with avg service 30ms, going from 50ms queue to 500ms adds 450ms to tail. So you quickly blow past 150ms target. That's why we include hard max_queue_ms and fast-fail or fallback policies
[00:12:55] Priya: do you support SLO-based autoscaling where if p99 breaches you trigger emergency scaling?
[00:13:02] Markus: yes  you can create SLO alarms that trigger scale actions and notify teams. We also support automated rollback on model-quality regressions detected by evals during rollout
[00:13:22] Ivy: let's talk instrumentation  what metrics should we export to our prometheus?
[00:13:28] Markus: export per-route RPS, per-GPU utilization, batch sizes, kv_cache_hit_rate, queue_length_ms, and token/sec. We also push scaling event logs and model variant selection logs
[00:13:50] Samir: about batch sizes  how do you avoid large batches causing latency spikes when sudden bursts arrive?
[00:13:57] Markus: dynamic batch sizing: cap max batch size and prefer latency-aware cutoffs; if queueing is high, prioritize smaller latency-critical requests and group background tasks separately
[00:14:20] Ben: for private on-prem, hardware choices  is it better to choose many smaller GPUs or fewer large GPUs?

[00:14:28] Markus: depends on model  larger models (70B+) often benefit from multi-GPU with NVLink, but discrete smaller GPUs give flexibility and lower per-instance cost. For high-concurrency small requests, more smaller GPUs can help because concurrency_per_gpu scales differently
[00:14:55] Lena: any notes on regional redundancy? we need multi-region failover for compliance

[00:15:02] Markus: yes; keep baseline in primary region and replicate minimal reserved in secondary. Use traffic weighting and automatic failover; KV caches are session-local so you may lose warm state on failover but functional correctness remains
[00:15:20] Priya: audit trail detail  do scaling events include who triggered and which policy?
[00:15:26] Ivy: yes  scaling events include policy id, triggering metric, and actor (auto vs manual). Logs are stored for your retention config
[00:15:40] Samir: let's run a hypothetical: 95% traffic is 128 tokens, 5% is 1k tokens. If we reserve for 95% and burst the 5%, how to measure impact?

[00:15:48] Markus: simulate in the spreadsheet  long requests occupy GPU longer and reduce concurrency for that period. We recommend isolating long-running jobs to separate pool with queue isolation so interactive flows aren't affected
[00:16:15] Ben: about billing  when burst spins up, how are costs reported and can we cap spend?
[00:16:20] Ivy: yes  billing shows reserved vs burst usage, and you can set upper bounds or alerts on burst spend. For Dedicated contracts we can add soft caps
[00:16:35] Lena: ok, couple of objections that typically come up: 1) operator fear of scaling oscillation; 2) inability to predict exact costs. How do you address these?

[00:16:45] Markus: oscillation  we use hysteresis, cooldowns, and multi-metric gating to avoid flip-flops. Cost predictability  baseline reserved gives predictable spend; we provide models showing expected burst costs under different percentiles
[00:17:10] Samir: can Redwood run a real benchmark with our traffic shape?

[00:17:15] Ivy: yes  next step: you share a small anonymized load trace and we'll run a capacity simulation and a short pilot with the recommended baseline. We can also run a hosted benchmark if you prefer
[00:17:35] Priya: legal needs a note on data residency for the burst pool  if burst runs in another region how is data handled?
[00:17:42] Markus: we can route bursts only to approved regions and ensure data-in-transit is encrypted; for strict residency you probably want on-prem or dedicated reserved
[00:17:58] Lena: talk about failover and graceful degradation when a model version regresses under load

[00:18:05] Markus: we recommend canary rollouts with canary traffic pinned to a small percentage and automatic rollback on latency/quality regressions; also fallback model routing to safe variant if quality drops
[00:18:28] Ben: any gotchas with KV cache persistence that bite people?

[00:18:33] Markus: yes  if you persist cache across restarts without eviction policy you can run out of memory; monitor kv_cache_size and set evictions. Also values stored should not contain PII unless you have appropriate controls
[00:18:55] Samir: how long should we keep warm standby vs scale up on demand?

[00:19:01] Markus: if peaks are predictable (scheduled), prefer pre-warm; if unpredictable keep small standby to avoid huge reserved cost. Our tooling can estimate break-even point based on historical peaks
[00:19:30] Ivy: we're going to demo a sample autoscale config now (screen share)  Markus walking through UI and YAML snippets
[00:19:40] [screen share walkthrough YAML examples, thresholds, fallback policy]
[00:23:10] Markus: note the policy: - min_replicas: 10, - scale_up_cpu_util_pct: 70, - scale_down_pct: 35, - max_queue_ms: 100, - batch_window_ms: route-specific
[00:24:00] Lena: how do we test this in staging without impacting prod?
[00:24:06] Ivy: create a staging project, reuse your org settings, and replay synthetic trace; we can also do a A/B traffic test
[00:24:30] Priya: question  are autoscale logs tamper-evident?
[00:24:36] Markus: logs are append-only and can be routed to your SIEM; for private deployments you can integrate HSM-backed signing if needed
[00:24:55] Samir: what's typical lead time to spin up reserved GPUs in Dedicated?
[00:25:00] Ivy: procurement dependent; reserving capacity usually takes 2-4 weeks for provisioning and networking, but we can sometimes do faster with cloud partners
[00:25:18] Ben: what's your recommended safety margin for reserved capacity?
[00:25:24] Markus: for p99 SLAs we use 15-25% headroom above estimated peak. For cost-conscious customers 10% may suffice but we see increased tail risk
[00:25:50] Lena: any notes on model sharding and cross-GPU latency?

[00:25:56] Markus: cross-GPU attention adds interconnect latency; for large shards pick NVLink-enabled instances to reduce that overhead. Also ensure batch sizing accounts for distributed decode overhead
[00:26:20] Ivy: wrapping up next section  practical pilot steps

[00:26:25] Markus: 1) share anonymized 7-day traffic trace; 2) Redwood runs capacity sim; 3) propose baseline reserved + burst config; 4) run 48h pilot with traffic replay; 5) review results and adjust
[00:26:50] Lena: ok good  timeline: we'd like findings in 10 days
[00:26:58] Ivy: we can commit to 10 business days once we have trace and CRM approval
[00:27:08] Samir: do you need a billing contact?
[00:27:12] Ivy: yes  please add billing contact to the spreadsheet, we'll include pricing scenarios
[00:27:25] Priya: action on security: please share SOC2 and KMS integration docs
[00:27:30] Ivy: will include security pack in follow-up
[00:27:45] Ben: small note  our ML team would like to test quantization variants for one model. Can we run evals during pilot?
[00:27:52] Markus: yes we can run automated evals and regression checks during the pilot, include those as part of deliverables
[00:28:10] Lena: any competitors to watch? sometimes our infra team asks about alternatives
[00:28:15] Ivy: we hear about Anthropic, OpenAI, in-house custom serving stacks  we'll include a short competitor note
[00:28:34] Samir: final technical Q  how do you handle backpressure on client side? do you expose queue depth?

[00:28:40] Markus: we expose queue_length_ms per request and recommend clients apply backoff and circuit-breaker: max latency threshold triggers fast-fail or fallback. We also provide client SDK helpers
[00:29:05] Lena: ok let's recap

[00:29:10] Ivy: recap: simulate with 7-day trace, propose baseline reserved+burst, pilot 48h, run evals including quant variants, share security docs, provide cost scenarios  deliver in 10 business days
[00:29:28] Priya: can you annotate the config with compliance notes?
[00:29:33] Markus: yes will annotate YAML and publish to shared doc
[00:29:48] Ben: thanks everyone, good session
[00:29:52] Ivy: thanks  we'll follow up with sheet and scheduler. meeting end
[00:30:00] [recording stopped]

Agreed next steps: share 7-day trace, run capacity sim, pilot with evals; deliverables in ~10 business days.
